figures.label: fig:study_area
figures.caption: **Figure 1. Population and modeled station locations in Alachua County.** Estimated 2025 population is divided by the total area of each 2020 census tract. Triangles show the 25 modeled 2025 station/base locations, with 23 engines and five quints. The dashed 2026 Gainesville boundary provides geographic context. The study covers 58 tracts, including 57 with positive baseline study-fire rates. The population-density map uses a logarithmic scale and UTM zone 17N.

figures.label: fig:policy_means
figures.caption: **Figure 3. Regional mean travel under PPO and stage greedy.** Circles and 95% intervals use 2,000 paired bootstrap samples of 15 whole event streams (seeds 101–115); diamonds show the saved fast-evaluator differences. The six scenario–year checks pair Medium trend (w = 1), High trend (w = 1), and High proportional growth (w = 0) with 2035 and 2045. D_F is the fixed-fire-rate-weighted standard deviation of tract mean fire travel; M_F and M_O are incident-level regional means for study-fire and other calls. Travel is en route to arrival. Negative differences favor PPO. The two trend configurations match in 2035; High proportional 2035 uses a different vehicle mix. All three 2045 regional mean contrasts favor PPO. Shared stage action-count limits allow different final fleets because a new station includes an engine. In 2045, PPO/greedy have 30/29 engines and 5/5 quints under Medium trend; 31/28 engines and 5/6 quints under High trend; and 30/29 engines and 6/6 quints under High proportional growth. The contrasts combine location, fleet-size, and fleet-type choices. Some other-call intervals are narrower than their markers.

figures.label: fig:spatial_policy_diff
figures.caption: **Figure 4. Local fire-travel consequences: PPO versus stage greedy.** The 2045 Medium scenario uses historical-trend population allocation (w = 1). Differences compare frozen PPO with stage greedy, using tract means pooled over 15 paired E1 event streams. Travel is first-arriving eligible vehicle travel from en route to arrival. Negative values favor PPO. The symmetric color range is ±120 s, shared with the other scenarios for this comparison. Annotations sum fixed baseline fire-rate weights in faster, slower, and unchanged tracts; differences within 10⁻¹⁰ min count as numerical equality. These categories use point estimates. The policies share stage action-count limits and select different final locations and fleets.

figures.label: fig:e2_growth
figures.caption: **Figure 5. Spatial growth and the engine-addition decision in E2.** The Medium county path uses historical-trend allocation (S1, w = 1). Triangles show the common configuration immediately after the shared GFR_01 relocation to C18. The subsequent vehicle decision chooses between A, adding an engine at the E62 modeled base, and B, adding an engine at CO_29. Gold marks the frozen PPO choice. Both states have the same county population and resource configuration; S0 applies uniform proportional growth and selects A, while S1 selects B. Their growth maps share the same scale. Fire rates remain fixed; population changes affect non-fire workload.

figures.label: fig:e2_case
figures.caption: **Figure 6. Action consequences in the matched E2 states.** A adds an engine at the E62 modeled base; B adds one at CO_29. S0 uses proportional growth (w = 0), and S1 uses historical-trend allocation (w = 1), with the same Medium county population and post-relocation resource configuration. Each point averages the 2040 and 2045 outcomes. Circles and 95% intervals use 2,000 paired bootstrap samples of 15 whole event streams (seeds 101–115); diamonds show the saved fast-evaluator differences. Each bootstrap sample uses the same stream indices in both years. D_F is the fixed-fire-rate-weighted standard deviation of tract mean fire travel; M_F and M_O are incident-level regional means for study-fire and other calls. Travel is en route to arrival. The frozen continuations all build at C12 and add an engine at CO_29 in 2040. The original fast reward favors A in S0 through a smaller other-call penalty, and B in S1 through lower dispersion with zero regional-mean penalties. The reward hinge starts at the exact 2025 baseline; the 0.05-min tolerance applies to violation reporting. Simulator D_F and M_F intervals cross zero in both states, while M_O favors A in both.

figures.label: fig:policy_results
figures.caption: **Figure S1. E1 differences in spatial fire-travel dispersion.** Circles and 95% intervals use 2,000 paired bootstrap samples of 15 whole event streams (seeds 101–115); diamonds show the saved fast-evaluator differences. The six scenario–year checks pair Medium trend (w = 1), High trend (w = 1), and High proportional growth (w = 0) with 2035 and 2045. D_F is the fixed-fire-rate-weighted standard deviation of tract mean fire travel; M_F and M_O are incident-level regional means for study-fire and other calls. Travel is en route to arrival. Negative differences favor PPO. The two trend configurations match in 2035; High proportional 2035 uses a different vehicle mix. All four nonidentical simulator dispersion intervals cross zero. Event-stream intervals describe variation within each scenario–year and exclude evaluator discrepancy.

figures.label: fig:spatial_consequences
figures.caption: **Figure S2. Local fire-travel consequences: PPO versus no action.** The 2045 Medium scenario uses historical-trend population allocation (w = 1). Differences compare frozen PPO with no action, using saved fast-evaluator tract means. Travel is first-arriving eligible vehicle travel from en route to arrival. Negative values favor PPO. The symmetric color range is ±160 s, shared with the other scenarios for this comparison. Annotations sum fixed baseline fire-rate weights in faster, slower, and unchanged tracts; differences within 10⁻¹⁰ min count as numerical equality. These categories use point estimates. No action retains the initial 25 locations and 28 vehicles.

figures.label: fig:growth_draws
figures.caption: **Figure S3. Policy contrasts across 48 held-out growth draws.** Squares show fast-evaluator differences in the mean of four evaluation years (2030, 2035, 2040, 2045), averaged over 48 held-out growth draws. Intervals are the existing 95% paired bootstrap intervals over whole draws. D_F is the fixed-fire-rate-weighted standard deviation of tract mean fire travel; M_F and M_O are incident-level regional means for study-fire and other calls. Travel is en route to arrival. Negative values favor PPO on the plotted metric. PPO has a larger D_F than stage greedy by 0.251 s (95% CI 0.164–0.332 s). These intervals describe growth-draw variation, distinct from the event-stream variation in E1.

figures.label: fig:fire_weights
figures.caption: **Figure S4. Spatial weights for study-fire demand.** Each tract contributes its share of the fixed study-fire rate estimated from October 2024–March 2025 incidents. Study-fire calls comprise outside, structure, vehicle, and brush fires; other calls form the remaining modeled call group. These shares are county demand weights, rather than per-resident risk rates. One of the 58 tracts has zero baseline fire rate. The scenarios retain these fire rates while non-fire workload changes with population. Triangles show the initial modeled station/base locations.

figures.label: fig:baseline_travel
figures.caption: **Figure S5. Baseline service under the 2030 Medium trend scenario.** The fast evaluator estimates first-arriving eligible engine/quint travel with the unchanged 2025 configuration and 2030 Medium historical-trend growth (w = 1). Travel is en route to arrival. The hatched tract has zero baseline fire rate and an undefined fire-travel mean. Triangles show the initial modeled station/base locations. The scenario keeps fire rates fixed and changes non-fire workload with population.
